10A General principles 
Students will be assessed on their ability to: 
 
10.1 be able to classify reactions (including those in Unit 1) as addition, elimination, substitution, 
oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis or polymerisation  
10.2 understand the concept of a reaction mechanism  
10.3 understand that heterolytic bond breaking results in species that are electrophiles or nucleophiles  
10.4 know the definition of the term ‘nucleophile’  
10.5 understand the link between bond polarity and the type of reaction mechanism a compound will   
         undergo  
10B: Halogenoalkanes 
10.6 understand the nomenclature of halogenoalkanes and be able to draw their        
         structural, displayed and skeletal formulae  
10.7 understand the distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes 
10.8 understand the reactions of halogenoalkanes with:  
    i  aqueous alkali, including KOH(aq) to produce alcohols(where the hydroxide ion acts as a nucleophile)  
 ii ethanolic potassium hydroxide to produce alkenes by an elimination reaction (where the hydroxide  
ion acts as a base) 
   iii aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol (where water acts as a nucleophile) 
   iv alcoholic ammonia under pressure to produce amines (where the ammonia acts as a nucleophile) 
   v  alcoholic potassium cyanide to produce nitriles (where the cyanide ion acts as a nucleophile) 
       Students should know this is an example of increasing the length of the carbon chain. 
10.9 understand the mechanisms of the nucleophilic substitution reactions between primary            
       halogenoalkanes and: 
   i   aqueous potassium hydroxide 
   ii  ammonia 
Note: SN1 and SN2 substitution mechanisms will be tested in Unit 4. 
10.10 understand that experimental observations and data can be used to compare the relative  
 
rates of hydrolysis of: 
  i    primary, secondary and tertiary structural isomers of a halogenoalkane 
  ii   primary chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes using aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol  
10.12  know the trend in reactivity of primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes  
10.13  understand, in terms of bond enthalpy, the trend in reactivity of chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes

10 B HALOGENOALKANES  
➢ Halogenoalkanes (also called haloalkanes) have a halogen atom attached to a hydrocarbon chain. 
➢ Halogenoalkanes have the general formula CnH2n+1X, where X is a halogen atom (F, Cl, Br or I) 
➢ The halogen atom may be at the end of the chain or on any of the carbons.  
➢ Halogenoalkanes have only single bonds in the molecule. 
 
Nomenclature 
In the IUPAC system, 
➢ Identify the longest chain of carbon atoms containing the halogen. 
➢ Halogen substituents are indicated by the prefixes fluoro, chloro, bromo and iodo, and are listed in 
alphabetical order with other substituents 
➢ The carbon number is also added to show the location of the halogen. 
➢ No locant is needed with only two carbons. 
➢ With longer chains, a locant is needed to tell us where on the chain the halogen atom is situated. 
 
Compound 
Name 
CH3Cl 
Chloromethane 
CH3CH2Br 
Bromoethane 
CH3CH2CH2I 
1-iodopropane 
CH3CH(I)CH3 
2-iodopropane 
 
➢ If the carbon chain is branched, the longest continuous carbon chain 
containing the halogen atom is given the parent name and the side chains 
are named as alkyl groups.  
 
➢ If there are more than one halogen atoms, di-, tri-, tetra-, etc. are used. In 
this case locants are used to say where they are.  
Eg. 
CH3CH(Cl) CH(Cl)CH3 
 
2,3-dichlorobutane

Isomers of Halogenoalkanes  
• 
Isomers are the organic compounds, which have the same molecular formula but different structural 
formula and properties. The phenomenon is called isomerism. 
• 
Haloalkanes can exhibit following type of isomerism. 
• 
Chain isomerism: occurs due to branching in carbon chains.     
 
• 
Position isomerism: occurs due to the position in which the functional group is present.

10B 
Reactivity of Halogenoalkanes 
          
➢ Halogens have a greater electronegativity than carbon. A dipole is induced in the C-X bond 
and it becomes polar, carbon is always δ+ and X is always δ-.  
 
➢ The polarity produces an electron deficient carbon atom, C δ+ which is 
important in the reactions of halogenoalkanes. Thus δ+ carbon can be 
attacked by nucleophiles.  
 
➢ All halogenoalkanes react with same reagent and undergo same type of reactions but the 
rate of reaction varies with two factors; 
1. Nature of halogen:  
Chloroalkane 
 
C---Cl 
 
 
 
Rate of the reaction increases 
because the carbon halogen 
bond becomes longer and 
hence weaker, so less energy 
required to break it. 
 
Bromoalkane 
 
C------Br 
 
Iodoalkane 
 
C----------I 
 
2. Type of halogenoalkane: 
           10Halogenoalkane                            20Halogenoalkane                             30Halogenoalkane 
 
 
Rate of the reaction increases 
 
➢ Rate of reaction increases due to the increase in stability of the carbocations.  
➢ Tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary carbocations which are more 
stable than primary carbocations.  
 
 
 
  Tertiary        >          Secondary       >          Primary      >          methyl

Reactions of Halogenoalkanes 
 
➢ Many organic reactions are very slow and the reagents used are volatile. For such reactions 
a process known as heating under reflux is used.  
➢ This technique involves boiling the reaction mixture and condensing the vapour produced 
back into the flask continuously, so that the heating process can be carried out for a longer 
period of time.  
Reaction with aqueous alkali 
Reagent:   
 
Aqueous Sodium hydroxide/ Aqueous potassium hydroxide 
Condition: 
 
Heat under reflux in aqueous solution 
Type of reaction:  
Nucleophilic Substitution  
Products:   
 
Alcohol

e.g. CH3CH2Br  + :OH-(aq)

Concentrated potassium hydroxide

10B 
Comparing the rates of Hydrolysis reactions 
 
Hydrolysis reactions 
Hydrolysis reaction is a reaction in which water or hydroxide ions replace an atom in a molecule 
with an -OH group. 
 
Equation : 
 RX + H2O →   ROH + HX  (R- represents an alkyl group and X is a halogen) 
or 
 RX + H2O →   ROH + H+  + X-  
 
Example: 
 CH3CH2Cl + H2O  CH3CH2OH + H+  + Cl-  
 
 
Reaction with water containing silver nitrate solution  
Experiment: To study the effect of different halogen atoms on the rate of hydrolysis 
 
➢ The halogen reacts with the water to form an alcohol and a solution that contains the 
halide ion. 
             CH3CH2X(aq)+ H2O(l)  → CH3CH2OH(aq) + H+(aq)  + X-(aq) 
 
  
➢ This halide ion then reacts with silver ions from the silver nitrate to form a precipitate of 
silver halide; 
   X-(aq)+  Ag+(aq)   
     AgX(s) 
Reagent:   
 
Water, Silver nitrate solution 
Condition: 
 
Room temperature and pressure 
Type of reaction:  
Hydrolysis 
Products:   
 
Alcohol 
Observation:    
White ppt (AgCl) – chloroalkane 
 
 
 
Cream ppt (AgBr) – bromoalkane 
 
 
 
Yellow ppt (AgI) – iodoalkane

Method:  
• To three test tubes, add aqueous silver nitrate (1 cm3) and ethanol (2 cm3) and place in a 
water bath at 600C. (Ethanol is added as a solvent to dissolve the halogenoalkane as it is 
insoluble in water.) 
• After five minutes, add 2 drops of chlorobutane to first tube, add 2 drops of bromobutane to 
the second tube and add 2 drops of Iodobutane to third tube. 
• Each test tube is shaken, loosely corked and observed at 600C for ten minutes.

10B Rates of hydrolysis for different halogenoalkane 
 
➢ Rate of hydrolysis can be compared by noting the time taken for the precipitate to appear; 
o Primary halogenoalkanes hardly react with water. 
o Secondary halogenoalkane reacts slowly to form a secondary alcohol and ppt is 
soon observed. 
o Tertiary halogenoakanes react rapidly to produce a tertiary alcohol. A precipitate is 
seen as soon as silver nitrate is added. 
This can be used as a test to identify the halogen in the halogenoalkane.

10B 
Nucleophilic Substitution mechanisms 
 
➢ In these reactions the attacking species is a nucleophile such as OH- ions and ammonia 
molecules. 
 
1. Nucleophilic substitution reaction between bromoethane and aqueous potassium hydroxide 
ions 
 
 
 
 
 
                                                                                                   Ethanol     
• Reaction starts by donating a lone pair of electrons from the oxygen of the hydroxide to 
the electron deficient carbon atom. 
• A C-O bond is formed and at the same time the electrons in C-Br move to Br atom and the 
C-Br bond breaks. 
• This type of bond breaking, where both electrons of the shared pair of electrons in a 
covalent bond are kept by one atom is called heterolytic fission.  
 
2. Nucleophilic substitution reaction between bromopropane and aqueous potassium hydroxide 
ions. 
 
 
 
→ 
 
                     Amino propane 
• First step - Reaction starts by donating a lone pair of electrons from nitrogen of the 
ammonia molecule to the electron deficient carbon atom. 
• A C-N bond is formed and at the same time the electrons in C-Br move to Br atom and the 
C-Br bond breaks. 
• Second step – Another ammonia molecule acting as a base, removes a hydrogen from the 
ion formed.
